This page covers the GM-side workflow — setting up NPCs, running combat, and managing Conditions.

NPCs and Adversaries

Create an NPC the same way as a Character — from the Actors sidebar tab's Create Actor button, set Type to NPC / Adversary. NPCs use the exact same Attributes/Skills/Resources/Wounds/Combat Dice mechanics as player characters (per the rules: "Game Masters will use those same rules when portraying adversaries"), just without the player-facing fluff (Concept, Career, Non-Combat Skills) — instead they get a Role tag (Minion/Standard/Elite/Nemesis) and a GM Notes field for tactics reminders. Leave NPC tokens unlinked (Foundry's default) so multiple copies of the same monster track wounds independently; Character tokens are force-linked instead, since a PC should always be the one actor.

Portrait Art vs. Token Art

Every Actor (Character or NPC) actually has two separate images: the sheet Portrait (click the art in the sheet header) and the canvas Token Image (what shows when you place it on a scene). Foundry copies the Portrait into the Token Image automatically exactly once — the very first time you set a new Actor's Portrait away from the default placeholder. After that first time, the two are completely independent: changing the Portrait later never touches the Token Image, and vice versa. Click the small pawn-icon button on the corner of the Portrait to set the Token Image directly, without leaving the sheet. Because NPC tokens are unlinked (see above), changing an NPC's Token Image only affects tokens you place after the change — copies already sitting on a scene keep whatever art they were dropped with; drag a fresh token from the sheet to pick up the update, or right-click the placed token → Configure Token to edit it individually.

Running Combat

Combat is driven entirely by Foundry's own Combat Tracker — add combatants, click Begin Combat, and advance rounds/turns from there. Every entry point that rolls Initiative (the tracker's per-combatant dice icon, its Roll All and Roll NPCs buttons, and each sheet's own Roll Initiative button) opens the same dice-commit dialog and produces identical results, so it doesn't matter which one you or your players use. Ending the encounter (deleting the Combat) automatically resets each combatant's combat-state flags and clears any Threads/Authority Specialties that expire at Encounter's end.

Conditions

Conditions live in the Conditions compendium and are also registered as Token HUD status icons — right-click a token, open the status-effects palette, and toggle a Condition on or off directly. This adds or removes a real owned Condition Item on the actor (with whatever mechanical Active Effect the rules define, e.g. Chilled's Movement -2), exactly the same as dragging the Condition Item onto the actor's sheet by hand — use whichever is more convenient in the moment.

Authoring New Content

If you have Foundry's "Create Items" permission (or are a GM), a wand-icon scene-control button opens the Create Content wizard for authoring new Action/Reaction Cards, Equipment, and Conditions straight into the compendium, without hand-building the data model yourself.

Compendiums

Action Cards, Reaction Cards, Conditions, and Equipment ship pre-populated from the live Essence Rules database; Species, Heritages, and Distinctions are hand-authored; and the Combat Styles Reference journal documents every Combat Skill's Specialty mechanic in full. See the system's README for how to refresh this content from the database if the rules change.

Every NPC has a Role tag — Minion, Standard, Elite, or Nemesis — but nothing in the printed rules defines what that tag actually means mechanically. The Monster Creator's Auto-Generate Stat Block needs something to generate from, so this system invents a budget: a plain, tunable table of numbers (kept in module/data/monster-budgets.mjs) that caps what you can hand-enter on a Monster and drives what Auto-Generate rolls up on its own. Treat every number here as homebrew, not canon — revisit it if actual play says a Role feels off.

The Tier Ladder

Four Roles, seven budget axes each. Every axis climbs by the same flat step from one Role to the next — no exponential curves — so you can eyeball roughly how much stronger the next Role up is without doing math. Total Combat Cards (Action + Reaction), for instance, lands on 1 → 3 → 5 → 7: a clean +2 every Role.

RoleAttributesSkillsResilienceTemp WoundsCards (A/R)Equipment
Minion2 pts, max 22 pts, max 21 + 1×Tier01 / 01
Standard7 pts, max 35 pts, max 33 + 2×Tier12 / 12
Elite10 pts, max 48 pts, max 45 + 3×Tier23 / 23
Nemesis13 pts, max 512 pts, max 57 + 4×Tier34 / 34

Resilience Scales With Tier

Resilience is the one axis that is a formula rather than a flat number, since a Tier 5 Minion shouldn't take the same hit before Wounds start as a Tier 1 one. Resilience = Base + Per-Tier × Tier, both of which climb with Role:

RoleTier 1Tier 3Tier 5
Minion246
Standard5913
Elite81420
Nemesis111927

How Auto-Generate Spends the Budget

The one-button path on the Concept step rolls the whole stat block in this order, then hands every result back to you to hand-edit exactly like the rest of the Monster Creator. Each step below also has its own Reroll button for redoing just that part.

  1. Attributes & Skills — a weighted point-buy: each point is a coin-flip weighted 3-to-1 toward whichever Domain you picked as the Emphasis (Physical/Mental/Spiritual), enough to lean the roll without ever locking the other two Domains out. Skills respect the same five Distinction gates a player would: Gestalt (requires Gifted), Magecraft (Arcanist), Psionics (Psyker), Ritualism (Invoker), and Calling (Summoner) only receive points if the matching Distinction is already attached.
  2. Resilience, Temporary Wounds, Equipment Limit — set directly from the Role/Tier budget table above, no randomness.
  3. Combat Cards — every owned Action/Reaction Card is cleared and re-picked from the qualifying pool, weighted 3-to-1 toward the three Skills the Attribute/Skill roll happened to land highest on, so a Nemesis that rolled heavy Ritualism tends to walk away with Ritualism cards.
  4. Equipment — a straight random draw from the Equipment compendium, capped at the Role's Equipment count.

Tuning It

Every number above is a plain object literal in module/data/monster-budgets.mjs — nothing else in the system reasons about the exact values, so any of them can be edited directly. A retuned number takes effect on the very next sheet opened; no migration, no data to rebuild.
